analysis.one_liner: Bans oil and gas seismic airgun testing along the Atlantic coast.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 11 cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing or vote in the Senate Energy Committee and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to ban geological and geophysical surveys — chiefly seismic airgun blasting — conducted to find oil, gas, or methane hydrates in the North Atlantic, Mid-Atlantic, South Atlantic, and Straits of Florida planning areas. Airgun surveys fire loud sound pulses into the seafloor and are the first step toward offshore drilling. The goal is to keep that exploration from ever starting along the Atlantic coast.
analysis.who_benefits: Atlantic coastal communities whose economies run on fishing and tourism, commercial fishermen whose catch depends on healthy marine life, and residents who live near or use the coast. Seismic airgun surveys produce intense, repeated underwater noise that can disturb or harm whales, dolphins, turtles, and fish populations, so barring them protects the marine resources those communities depend on.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Atlantic fishing and coastal tourism communities

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any person or federal agency from conducting geological or geophysical activities — the category that includes deep-penetration seismic airgun surveys — in support of oil, gas, or methane hydrate exploration and development in four Atlantic planning areas of the outer Continental Shelf.

Writes the ban into the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act itself and states it applies 'notwithstanding any other provision of law,' so it would override any future administration's decision to permit the surveys rather than leaving protection to agency discretion.

Shields marine mammals, fisheries, and the coastal economies that rely on them from airgun blasting: the bill's declared subjects include mammals, marine and coastal resources, fisheries, and wildlife habitat, and the surveys it bans are the loud sound-pulse tests used to search for offshore oil and gas.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies and seismic survey contractors that want to explore the Atlantic outer Continental Shelf would lose legal access to it, and the federal treasury would forgo any future drilling royalties that exploration could have led to. Supporters of domestic energy production would also argue the country forgoes information about what resources lie offshore.
analysis.who_pays_short: Offshore oil and gas exploration companies

drawbacks.text: The moratorium is sweeping: it permanently bars energy exploration across four large Atlantic planning areas with no exception process, foreclosing any future domestic oil and gas development, associated jobs, and federal royalty revenue from those waters.

Because it applies 'notwithstanding any other provision of law,' the ban leaves no room for agencies to approve a survey case by case — for example, with conditions designed to reduce harm to marine life — even if a future administration judged the risks manageable.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill protects the fishing grounds, marine life, and tourism assets that Atlantic coastal economies run on by stopping the loudest and most invasive form of offshore energy exploration before it starts. The cost falls on oil and gas companies and their contractors, plus the foregone possibility of discovering and developing Atlantic oil and gas. How large that cost is depends on how much recoverable oil and gas is actually out there — no commercial production was underway in these waters — but the trade is real, and the ban's absolute, no-exception design means no compromise for survey methods with smaller impacts.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never gave it a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Cory Booker introduced the bill on March 14, 2019, joined by ten cosponsors — ten Democrats and one independent — all from his party's caucus, including several from Atlantic coastal states such as New Jersey, Connecticut, Delaware, New Hampshire, Maryland, Massachusetts, and New York.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, which handles offshore energy matters.
No further action ever appears in the bill's history: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote. It sat in committee until the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, at which point it expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas exploration interests are better off: the legal path to seismic surveying and potential drilling in the Atlantic remained open, unchanged, while coastal communities gained no new protection against blasting.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore oil and gas exploration interests

for.name: Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and rounded up the chamber's coastal-state Democrats as cosponsors.

for.name: Ten Democratic senators and one independent
for.role: Cosponsors, including Sens. Blumenthal, Whitehouse, Menendez, Shaheen, Warren, Hassan, Cardin, Markey, Gillibrand, and Sanders (I-VT)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it a full complement of Atlantic-coast support but no Republican backers.

against.name: Lisa Murkowski
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it; it received no action for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Offshore oil and gas industry
against.role: Exploration companies, seismic survey contractors, and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Supported keeping Atlantic waters open for seismic surveying and drilling and opposed legislative bans on the activity.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's independents, no Republican signed on, and the Republican-led Energy Committee let the bill sit without action for nearly two years.

industries.industry: Offshore oil and gas exploration and seismic survey contractors
industries.note: Seismic airgun surveys are the first step toward offshore drilling, and the bill makes them illegal in the Atlantic planning areas outright. Industry loses the option to open a new exploration frontier; the public avoids underwater noise that threatens whales, dolphins, and fish stocks.

industries.industry: Atlantic commercial fishing and coastal tourism
industries.note: Fishing businesses and beach-dependent tourism economies depend on healthy marine mammal and fish populations and an undisturbed ocean. By blocking airgun blasting, the bill removes a threat to those resources; the subjects list covers fisheries, mammals, and wildlife habitat.
